*"Dynamic Programming is hard..." many a SWE interview candidate*

# Introduction
I am far from a competititve programmer and perhaps that will make my explanations and examples more amenable to the non-initiated. I never came across Dynamic Programming (or more generally Backwards Induction) in my Physics undergrad so it was quite unfamiliar turf when I started learning. Ironically I now quite enjoy these types of problems as a “respite” from the more mathematically involved stuff that comes up in my studies. Anyhow, I am far from the first to have had the rude awakening at some point that without a little practice, you can be great at a lot of maths and suck at Dynamic Programming – [here](https://www.reddit.com/r/learnprogramming/comments/3tz9a3/is_it_just_me_or_is_dynamic_programming_very/) is an old subreddit on the topic.

Over the year or so, I’ve been accruing a bank of problems I’ve quite liked, simple problems that don’t require textbook proofs. Eventually I want to make all these problems and their worked solutions available on my website in a perhaps more organised format than a blog post. As an introduction to the educational blogpost genre, I want to tackle Dynamic Programming.

# The Bellman Equation
A quick scroll through [Richard Bellman’s](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Bellman) wikipedia is a good place to start to get a sense of where Dynamic Programming (and its modern much more involved counterpart, Reinforcement Learning) come from. We label states as $s \in \mathcal{S}$ and for every state we can define a set of valid actions $\mathcal{A}(s)$. We then define two useful functions:

1. The optimal state value function $V(s)$
2. The action value function $Q(a; s)$ -- where we write $(a; s)$ as a notational reminder that $a \in \mathcal{A}(s)$ and there is a dependence on the state
3. The state transition function $T(s, a)$

The idea proposed by Bellman is that we should seek an “optimal substructure”. This natively lends itself to a recursive definition which I think makes most sense in form of an equation:

$$
\begin{equation}
V(s) = \max_{a \in \mathcal{A}(s)} \{ Q(a; s) + V(T(s, a)) \}
\end{equation}
$$

Breaking the equation up, it says:

*“The action defining the optimal value at state s is the action which takes you to the neighbouring state with maximal optimal value”*
